prompt_instruction: Click the sentence that states the warrant: the general rule that bridges the data to the claim.

passage_segments.text: Priya has shipped every release on time for two years.
She should lead the migration project.
Anyone who reliably hits their own deadlines will handle a cross-team project well.
The board meets on Thursday to confirm the appointment.

options.text: Shipping your own work on time doesn't show you can coordinate other teams.
options.feedback: Yes. The rule leaps from individual reliability to cross-team leadership, which is a different skill.

options.text: Two years isn't a long enough track record.
options.feedback: That challenges the data, not the bridge rule.

options.text: Priya might not want the job.
options.feedback: Possibly true, but it doesn't touch the argument's logic.

options.text: The board might not meet on Thursday.
options.feedback: Context, not argument.

explanation_formal: Sentence 1 is the Data, sentence 2 the Claim, and sentence 3 the Warrant, the general rule licensing the step from one to the other. Sentence 4 is circumstantial context.
explanation_modern: Fact: she's always on time. Claim: she should lead. Bridge: punctual people make good project leads. The bridge is where to aim, because punctuality and leadership aren't the same thing.

prompt_instruction: This argument skips a step. Click the sentence whose conclusion depends most on an unstated premise.

passage_segments.text: The new cycle lane on Mill Road has cut car traffic by a fifth.
So the council should build cycle lanes on every arterial road in the city.
passage_segments.note: Rests on the unstated premise that Mill Road's result generalises.

passage_segments.text: Residents on Mill Road report that the street is quieter.
Shopkeepers there were sceptical at first.

options.text: What worked on Mill Road will work about as well on every arterial road.
options.feedback: Right. The jump from one road to all of them is the silent premise doing the heavy lifting.

options.text: Cycling is healthier than driving.
options.feedback: The argument never relies on health. It's a plausible belief, but not the missing step.

options.text: Every resident of the city owns a bicycle.
options.feedback: Far stronger than the argument needs, so it isn't the hidden premise.

options.text: Shopkeepers' opinions don't matter.
options.feedback: Sentence 4 is context. The conclusion doesn't depend on dismissing anyone.

explanation_formal: An enthymeme: from a single case (Mill Road) to a universal policy. The suppressed major premise, roughly 'interventions that succeed on one road succeed on all similar roads', is where the argument can be challenged.
explanation_modern: One success story, then 'do it everywhere'. The silent premise is that every road is like Mill Road. Say it out loud and you can test it.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence where the speaker shifts from Forensic (past blame) to Deliberative (future choice).

passage_segments.text: Last quarter's outage happened because nobody reviewed the config change.
The on-call rota was understaffed, and the runbook was two years out of date.
From next sprint, let's require a second reviewer on every production config change.
That should make another outage like this far less likely.

explanation_formal: Sentences 1–2 are forensic: causes and fault in the past. Sentence 3 turns to the deliberative genre by proposing a future action, and sentence 4 argues its advantage.
explanation_modern: The first two sentences ask whose fault it was. The third asks what we do now. That's where the argument starts producing decisions instead of defensiveness.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence doing Demonstrative work, praising present values, rather than recounting the past or proposing action.

passage_segments.text: Fifteen years ago this library was a derelict warehouse with a leaking roof.
A group of volunteers raised the money, rewired the building and stocked the shelves.
They are the kind of neighbours every town claims to have and few towns actually do.
Next spring the council will vote on whether to fund an extension.

explanation_formal: Sentences 1–2 narrate past events, sentence 4 looks to a future decision, and sentence 3 is epideictic: present-tense praise that defines the community's values.
explanation_modern: Sentence 3 is the 'this is who we are' line. It bonds the room around a value, and that's what makes the later vote easier to win.

prompt_instruction: Triage this dispute in three steps.

passage_segments.text: Manager: “We didn't fire Sam. We just didn't renew his contract.”
Union rep: “Ending a three-year rolling contract without warning is a dismissal in all but name.”
Both sides agree the contract ended on 31 March and that Sam had no warning.

steps.label: Stasis
steps.question: At which stasis is this dispute stuck?

options.text: Conjecture: did it happen?
options.feedback: The facts are agreed in sentence 3.

options.text: Definition: what do we call what happened?
options.feedback: Yes. Same facts, competing labels: 'non-renewal' versus 'dismissal'.

options.text: Quality: how bad was it?
options.feedback: Nobody is arguing severity yet. They can't, until they agree what it was.

options.text: Policy: what should be done?
options.feedback: Remedies come later, once the label is settled.

steps.label: Resolving question
steps.question: Which question, if answered, would actually move this dispute forward?

options.text: Under our agreement, what makes a non-renewal count as a dismissal?
options.feedback: Right. Agree the criteria, then apply them to the facts.

options.text: Did the contract really end on 31 March?
options.feedback: Already agreed. That's reopening conjecture for nothing.

options.text: Was Sam a good employee?
options.feedback: A quality question that doesn't settle the label.

options.text: Should the company rehire Sam?
options.feedback: Premature. Policy depends on the definition.

steps.label: Counter-pivot
steps.question: Choose the union rep's strongest next line.

options.text: You fired him, and you know it.
options.feedback: Bare contradiction. It restates the label without giving a reason.

options.text: Let's agree what counts as dismissal under our agreement. If three years of rolling renewals meet that test, we talk about reinstatement or compensation.
options.feedback: This proposes the criteria test and links it straight to a future remedy.

options.text: You did exactly the same to two people last year.
options.feedback: Drags the argument back into forensic blame.

options.text: Any decent employer would be ashamed of this.
options.feedback: An ethos attack. It raises the temperature and settles nothing.

explanation_formal: With conjecture conceded, the dispute sits at the stasis of definition. Progress requires agreed definitional criteria, after which the argument can ascend to quality and policy.
explanation_modern: They agree on what happened and fight over the word for it. Agree what the word means, check the facts against it, then talk remedies.

prompt_instruction: Each sentence argues at a different stasis. Click the one at the stasis of Conjecture (did it happen?).

passage_segments.text: The question isn't whether the leak was serious. Of course it was.
What matters is whether any customer data actually left our network.
Calling it a 'breach' before we know that is premature.
Either way, we should notify the regulator today.

follow_up_question.question: Which stasis does sentence 3 work at?

options.text: Definition
options.feedback: Yes. It argues about the right label ('breach') for the facts.

options.text: Quality
options.feedback: Severity was sentence 1.

options.text: Policy
options.feedback: Policy is sentence 4: notify the regulator.

options.text: Conjecture
options.feedback: It depends on conjecture, but it is arguing about the name.

explanation_formal: One stasis per sentence: quality (1), conjecture (2), definition (3), policy (4). Note how sentence 4 sidesteps the uncertainty: a policy that holds whatever conjecture resolves to.
explanation_modern: Did it happen (2)? What do we call it (3)? How bad is it (1)? What do we do (4)? The neat trick is the last line: an action that's right whichever way the facts fall.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence that states the Toulmin Rebuttal: the condition under which the claim would fail.

passage_segments.text: Our load tests show the new service handles 4,000 requests per second.
That's double our peak traffic, so it will almost certainly cope with Black Friday.
That holds unless the payment provider's API slows down, as it did last year, and requests start to queue.
Either way, we'll have engineers on call that weekend.

follow_up_question.question: Which phrase in sentence 2 is the Qualifier?

options.text: “almost certainly”
options.feedback: Right. The qualifier sets how strongly the claim is held.

options.text: “double our peak traffic”
options.feedback: That's data, restated.

options.text: “so”
options.feedback: An inference marker, not a qualifier.

options.text: “Black Friday”
options.feedback: The scenario, not the strength of the claim.

explanation_formal: Data (1) → Claim with Qualifier 'almost certainly' (2) → Rebuttal or Reservation stating the exception (3). Sentence 4 is contingency planning, not part of the argument structure.
explanation_modern: 'Almost certainly' says how sure. 'Unless the payment API slows' says when it breaks. Stating both makes you more believable, not less.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence that provides Backing: support for the warrant itself, rather than more data about this case.

passage_segments.text: The inspection found hairline cracks in three of the bridge's support beams.
Cracks like these mean the beams are fatiguing and will need replacing within five years.
That rule comes from forty years of the agency's own inspection records on steel bridges of this design.
So the replacement should go into this year's capital budget.

follow_up_question.question: What job does the backing do?

options.text: It supports the general rule linking cracks to replacement.
options.feedback: Yes. Backing answers 'why trust that bridge rule?'

options.text: It adds more evidence about this particular bridge.
options.feedback: That would be data. Backing is about the rule, not the case.

options.text: It qualifies how certain the claim is.
options.feedback: That's the qualifier's job.

options.text: It answers an objection.
options.feedback: That's a rebuttal. No objection has been raised.

explanation_formal: Toulmin distinguishes Data (facts of the case) from Backing (grounds for the warrant). Sentence 3 backs the warrant in sentence 2 with an inductive record.
explanation_modern: Sentence 2 is the rule. Sentence 3 says why the rule deserves trust: forty years of records. When someone challenges your rule, that's what you reach for.

prompt_instruction: Test the formal validity of this argument.

passage_segments.text: All certified auditors have passed the ethics exam.
Dana has passed the ethics exam.
Therefore, Dana is a certified auditor.

options.text: Valid: the conclusion follows from the premises.
options.feedback: The premises allow Dana to have passed the exam without being certified.

options.text: Invalid: the middle term ('passed the ethics exam') is never distributed.
options.feedback: Correct. Passing is necessary for certification, not sufficient.

options.text: Invalid, because the first premise is false.
options.feedback: Truth and validity are different questions. Validity is about form alone.

options.text: Valid but unsound.
options.feedback: It isn't valid in the first place.

steps.label: Counterexample
steps.question: Which argument has the same form and plainly fails?

options.text: All cats are mammals. Dogs are mammals. Therefore dogs are cats.
options.feedback: Same form, true premises, false conclusion. That proves the form is invalid.

options.text: All cats are mammals. Tom is a cat. Therefore Tom is a mammal.
options.feedback: That's a valid form (Barbara).

options.text: No fish are mammals. Whales are mammals. Therefore whales are not fish.
options.feedback: Valid (Cesare).

options.text: Some birds can't fly. Penguins are birds. Therefore penguins can't fly.
options.feedback: Different form (and invalid for another reason).

steps.label: Reply
steps.question: What would a careful colleague say?

options.text: Passing the exam is required for certification but doesn't prove it. We'd need to check Dana's certification itself.
options.feedback: Necessary versus sufficient, stated plainly, with the obvious next step.

options.text: Dana seems trustworthy, so it's probably fine.
options.feedback: Swaps logic for impression.

options.text: The ethics exam is too easy anyway.
options.feedback: A red herring. It's irrelevant to the inference.

options.text: Your first premise is wrong.
options.feedback: The premise is fine. The problem is the form.

explanation_formal: Form: All A are B; x is B; therefore x is A. This is the fallacy of the undistributed middle, a categorical cousin of affirming the consequent.
explanation_modern: Every auditor passed the exam. That doesn't mean everyone who passed is an auditor. Required isn't the same as enough.

prompt_instruction: Test the validity of this argument, then reason about it.

passage_segments.text: Every member of the review panel has read the proposal.
Jordan hasn't read the proposal.
So Jordan isn't on the panel.

options.text: Valid: if every member read it and Jordan didn't, Jordan can't be a member.
options.feedback: Yes. Denying the consequent of a universal is valid.

options.text: Invalid: undistributed middle.
options.feedback: Compare the auditor drill. Here the form is All A are B; x is not B; so x is not A. That form is valid.

options.text: Invalid: it affirms the consequent.
options.feedback: It denies the consequent, which is the valid direction.

options.text: Can't tell without knowing whether Jordan is diligent.
options.feedback: Validity is decided by form alone.

steps.label: If the conclusion is false
steps.question: Suppose Jordan is in fact on the panel. What must be true?

options.text: One of the premises is false. Perhaps not every member has actually read it.
options.feedback: Right. In a valid argument a false conclusion means a false premise. Here the universal premise is the likeliest suspect.

options.text: The argument was invalid after all.
options.feedback: Validity doesn't change with the facts.

options.text: Jordan must have read it secretly.
options.feedback: That's one way premise 2 could be false, but not the only possibility.

options.text: Nothing follows.
options.feedback: Something does: at least one premise is false.

explanation_formal: All A are B; x is not B; therefore x is not A. This is valid. A false conclusion would therefore show the falsity of a premise, usually the universal one.
explanation_modern: If everyone on the panel read it and Jordan didn't, Jordan isn't on the panel. If Jordan is on it, then 'everyone read it' was the bit that wasn't true.

register_tags.modern: What They Want You to Accept

prompt_instruction: Click the main Claim, the conclusion this passage is pushing.

passage_segments.text: Our main competitor cut prices by 15% in March.
Since then, three of our largest clients have asked for discounts.
We need to rethink our pricing before the renewal season.
Clients who see a cheaper equivalent tend to leave at renewal unless they're given a reason to stay.
Clients locked into multi-year integrations may be the exception.

options.text: Sentence 4: clients who see a cheaper equivalent tend to leave at renewal…
options.feedback: Yes. It's the general rule that turns the price cut into a threat.

options.text: Sentence 1: the competitor cut prices.
options.feedback: Data.

options.text: Sentence 2: clients asked for discounts.
options.feedback: Data.

options.text: Sentence 5: multi-year clients may be the exception.
options.feedback: That's the rebuttal or reservation.

explanation_formal: Data (1, 2), Claim (3), Warrant (4), Rebuttal (5). The claim sits mid-passage. Claims are identified by function, not position.
explanation_modern: Ask 'what do they want me to do or believe?' Here it's 'rethink pricing' in the middle. Everything else is a reason, a rule or an exception.

prompt_instruction: A meeting is going sideways. Diagnose it and choose your line.

passage_segments.text: We're going to miss the June delivery date we promised the client.
Colleague: “Whose idea was it to promise them June in the first place?”

steps.label: Tense
steps.question: Which tense is the colleague pulling the meeting into?

options.text: Forensic: past blame
options.feedback: Yes. 'Whose idea was it' is a question about fault.

options.text: Deliberative: future choice
options.feedback: Nothing in the question points forward.

options.text: Demonstrative: present values
options.feedback: It isn't praise or blame of character in the present.

options.text: None. It's a neutral question.
options.feedback: Tone aside, its function is assigning blame.

steps.label: Cost
steps.question: What's the main cost of following that question right now?

options.text: It turns a scheduling decision into a blame contest, and everyone gets defensive.
options.feedback: Right. The forensic tense breeds defence, not decisions.

options.text: It's rude.
options.feedback: Maybe, but the bigger cost is strategic, not social.

options.text: We'll never find out who made the promise.
options.feedback: We probably could. It just doesn't help us now.

options.text: There's no cost. Accountability matters most.
options.feedback: Accountability has a place (the retro), but the decision is due now.

options.text: It was the sales team, obviously.
options.feedback: You've joined the blame game.

options.text: That's irrelevant, and you know it.
options.feedback: Snark costs you ethos and offers no direction.

options.text: Fair question for the retro. Right now the choice is whether we ask for two more weeks or cut scope. Which costs the client less?
options.feedback: Concede-and-pivot: you grant the question its place, then put a concrete choice on the table.

options.text: We all share responsibility for what happened.
options.feedback: A demonstrative platitude. It leaves the meeting with no decision.

explanation_formal: Forensic questions in a deliberative setting displace the stasis from policy to fault. The remedy is to concede the forensic question a proper forum, then restore the deliberative tense with a concrete alternative.
explanation_modern: Blame can wait for the retro. The meeting's job is the choice, so name it, frame it as options, and ask the room to pick.

prompt_instruction: Assemble a single sentence that runs Data → Warrant → Qualified Claim → Rebuttal. One block is a decoy.

blocks.text: Because churn doubled after the price rise,
and customers who leave over price rarely come back,
unless the extra revenue more than covers the losses.

explanation_formal: Data (churn doubled), Warrant (price-driven churn is persistent), Claim with Qualifier ('probably'), Rebuttal ('unless…'). The decoy offers an over-general emotional premise in place of a warrant.
explanation_modern: Fact, rule, careful conclusion, escape hatch. The decoy ('everyone hates price rises') sounds like a reason, but it's a feeling stated as a rule.

prompt_instruction: Diagnose the speaker's move, then choose the best reply.

passage_segments.text: Yes, the intern copied two paragraphs from a blog into the report without attribution.
Yes, that's plagiarism.
But it was an internal draft, it was her first week, and nobody outside the team saw it.

steps.label: Stasis
steps.question: At which stasis is the speaker choosing to fight?

options.text: Conjecture
options.feedback: Conceded in sentence 1.

options.text: Definition
options.feedback: Conceded in sentence 2.

options.text: Quality
options.feedback: Yes. The facts and the label are granted, and the fight is over severity.

options.text: Policy
options.feedback: No remedy has been proposed yet.

steps.label: Flaw
steps.question: A colleague replies: “Plagiarism is plagiarism. Rules are rules.” What's wrong with that?

options.text: It's a tautology that repeats the definition and never engages with severity.
options.feedback: Right. It answers a quality argument with a definitional truism.

options.text: It's an ad hominem.
options.feedback: It doesn't attack anyone personally.

options.text: It's a slippery slope.
options.feedback: No chain of consequences is asserted.

options.text: Nothing. It's decisive.
options.feedback: It can't be decisive. Everyone already agreed it was plagiarism.

steps.label: Counter-pivot
steps.question: Choose the reply that is firm, fair and forward-looking.

options.text: If we let this slide, next year every intern will be copying whole reports.
options.feedback: A slippery slope, the Wrong Ending.

options.text: Agreed, the harm here is small. Let's treat it as a training moment and make attribution part of every intern's induction.
options.feedback: Grants the quality argument and turns it into a policy that prevents a repeat.

options.text: Her manager should have caught it.
options.feedback: Moves the blame sideways. Still forensic.

options.text: She clearly doesn't respect the team.
options.feedback: Mind-reading, and it escalates.

explanation_formal: A classic mitigation: concede conjecture and definition to contest quality. Responding with a definitional tautology misses the stasis. The productive response accepts the quality judgement and ascends to policy.
explanation_modern: She's not saying 'I didn't' or 'it isn't plagiarism'. She's saying 'it's minor'. Meet her there, then move to what changes next time.

prompt_instruction: Click the conclusion that rests on an unstated premise.

passage_segments.text: The new hire's code passed every automated test.
So it's ready to merge into the main branch.
passage_segments.note: Assumes the tests cover everything that matters.

passage_segments.text: The test suite runs on every commit.
It takes about twelve minutes to finish.

follow_up_question.question: Which premise is assumed but never stated?

options.text: Passing the automated tests is enough to show code is ready to merge.
options.feedback: Yes. And it's often false: tests rarely cover design, security or readability.

options.text: New hires write worse code than experienced staff.
options.feedback: Nobody says that, and the argument doesn't need it.

options.text: Twelve minutes is an acceptable build time.
options.feedback: Irrelevant to whether the code is ready.

options.text: The tests run on every commit.
options.feedback: That's stated in sentence 3, so it isn't silent.

explanation_formal: From 'passed tests' to 'ready to merge' requires the suppressed premise that test coverage is sufficient evidence of readiness, which is the point to contest.
explanation_modern: 'It passed the tests, so it's ready' quietly assumes the tests check everything. Say that out loud and the gap is obvious.

register_tags.modern: Put the Choice on the Table

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence that puts a concrete choice before the audience.

passage_segments.text: The previous administration sold the playing fields, and that was a mistake.
I'm not going to pretend otherwise.
But blaming them won't give one child a place to play next summer.
Leasing the school grounds at weekends will, and we can approve that tonight.

explanation_formal: Forensic concession (1–2), pivot naming the futility of blame (3), and a deliberative proposal with a concrete action and timeframe (4).
explanation_modern: Sentence 3 turns the corner, but sentence 4 is the choice: lease the school grounds, vote tonight. A pivot without an offer is only half a pivot.

prompt_instruction: Click the sentence that locates the live disagreement at the stasis of Policy.

passage_segments.text: Everyone agrees the waiting list for assessments is too long.
And we all accept that it has grown every year since 2019.
The live question is whether we hire more assessors or change who qualifies for an assessment.
Hiring is slow; changing the criteria is quick but fairer to some and harsher to others.

explanation_formal: Conjecture (2) and quality (1) are agreed, so the dispute advances to policy (3). Sentence 4 begins weighing the policy alternatives.
explanation_modern: Facts agreed, badness agreed, so the real argument is what to do. Naming that out loud stops people re-arguing the settled parts.
